hook: Salerno to the Po Valley — twenty long months in the Italian mountains, told slowly, for sleep.
narration:
Tonight, we go to Italy. We follow the war through twenty long months in the Italian mountains, from a beach in the Bay of Salerno, in September of nineteen forty-three, to a flat green river valley in the north of the country, in the spring of nineteen forty-five. The story is told slowly, the way it was told the first time. Calm, third-person, in the voice of an evening, with the lights low. There is nothing here you need to remember. The names of the rivers, the names of the towns, the names of the men — they will pass through the story and they will not be tested. You are welcome to drift, to come and go, to fall asleep at any time. The story will keep itself.

A word about the geography, before we start. Italy is a long country, shaped, as everyone has said for centuries, like a boot. The boot points down and to the south, into the middle of the Mediterranean. The toe of the boot is a few miles from Sicily, and Sicily is a few hundred miles from the coast of North Africa. To anyone planning a war from the south, Italy is the first place a foot can be set on the European mainland. The boot is also long. From the toe to the top of the leg is more than seven hundred miles. And the boot has a spine. A range of mountains called the Apennines runs the entire length of the country, from the toe to the Alps in the far north. The mountains are not very high, by the standards of the Alps or the Rockies, but they are steep and rocky, and they are cut every few miles by a river that runs from the mountains to the sea. For an army moving north, every river is a defensive line, and every range of hills is a defensive line, and the country itself is a long series of defensive lines, one after the other, all the way to the Po Valley in the north. The Germans, who hold Italy in the autumn of nineteen forty-three, understand this very well. The Allies, who land at the foot of the boot in September of that year, will come to understand it as well, slowly, over the months and the years that follow.

The weather in Italy, in the months we are speaking of, is not the gentle Mediterranean weather of the postcards. From October until April, in the mountains, it rains, and it snows, and the rivers come up over their banks, and the trails turn to mud the color of wet cement. The mud is deep enough that a jeep cannot drive through it. It is deep enough that mules sink to their bellies. The mud, in the memoirs of the men who fought there, is mentioned almost as often as the Germans. There is mud in November, mud in December, mud in January and February, mud in March. And then there is the snow. In the high passes, the snow lies four and five feet deep on the upper slopes. Soldiers learn to sleep in foxholes lined with straw. They learn to keep their rifles inside their coats so the bolts will not freeze. They learn that the warmest place in winter, in Italy, is two men in a single bedroll. The Italian campaign is not, despite what was said before it began, a soft campaign.

We begin the story in the spring of nineteen forty-three. The war in North Africa has just ended. The German and Italian armies in Tunisia have surrendered. A quarter of a million prisoners have been taken. The southern shore of the Mediterranean, from Casablanca to the Suez, is in Allied hands. At a conference in Casablanca, in January of that year, the British Prime Minister, Winston Churchill, and the American President, Franklin Roosevelt, have decided what to do next. The cross-channel invasion of France, which Roosevelt's generals want, is not yet ready. The landing craft are not built. The men are not trained. France will have to wait another year. In the meantime, the Allies have a great army in North Africa, and they cannot leave it idle. They will use it to invade Sicily, and from Sicily, they will move on to the Italian mainland, and from the Italian mainland, they will draw German divisions away from the Russian front and from the eventual fight in France. This is the strategy that Churchill calls, in a famous phrase, the soft underbelly of Europe. The phrase is reassuring. It is not, as the men who fight in Italy will learn, accurate.

The invasion of Sicily begins on the tenth of July, nineteen forty-three. Two Allied armies — the American Seventh, under General George Patton, and the British Eighth, under General Bernard Montgomery — land on the southern coast of the island, on a long crescent of beach from Licata in the west to Syracuse in the east. The landings, which involve nearly three thousand ships and one hundred and sixty thousand men, are the largest amphibious operation the world has ever seen. They will not hold that title for long. Eleven months later, the Normandy landings will be larger again. But on the tenth of July, nineteen forty-three, what comes ashore on the Sicilian coast is the largest invasion fleet ever assembled. The Italian coastal divisions defending the beaches do not, on the whole, fight hard. Many of them surrender almost immediately. The two German divisions on the island — the Hermann Göring Division and the Fifteenth Panzergrenadier — fight a long and skillful delaying action, falling back from the southern coast through the central highlands toward the Strait of Messina in the northeast.

The campaign in Sicily lasts thirty-eight days. The British Eighth Army moves up the eastern side of the island, through the towns at the foot of Mount Etna, against the heaviest German resistance. The American Seventh Army, on Patton's order, swings north and west, taking Palermo on the twenty-second of July, and then turns east along the northern coast toward Messina. The two armies arrive at Messina in early August. The strait between Sicily and the Italian mainland is only two miles wide. The Germans, having put up their long delaying fight, withdraw across the strait. The Allies, who have not prepared a closing operation — who have not, in particular, used their air power or their naval power to seal the strait — do not stop them. The Germans take across nearly all of their men and most of their equipment. They will be heard from again, in the months that follow, on every river and every mountain pass that the Allies must cross. The lesson of Messina, that an enemy who is allowed to withdraw will fight again on the next line, is one that the planners of the Italian campaign will learn slowly, over many months.

While Sicily is being taken, in the city of Rome, the Italian government collapses. On the night of the twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth of July, nineteen forty-three, the Fascist Grand Council votes against Benito Mussolini, the man who has ruled Italy for twenty-one years. The next morning, the King of Italy, Victor Emmanuel the Third, dismisses Mussolini and has him arrested. Mussolini is taken, by motorcade, to a remote hotel high in the Apennine mountains, where he is held under guard while the new government decides what to do with him. A new government is formed in Rome, under an old soldier named Pietro Badoglio. Badoglio assures the Germans, in public, that Italy will continue the war on their side. In private, he begins negotiating, secretly, with the Allies. The Germans, who do not entirely believe the public statement, begin moving more divisions into northern Italy, just in case. By the end of August, there are sixteen German divisions on Italian soil, on top of the divisions already withdrawn from Sicily. They are positioned, very deliberately, near the major cities and the major roads. If Italy switches sides, the Germans intend to occupy the country in a matter of days.

The negotiations between Badoglio and the Allies take more than a month. They are conducted in Lisbon, in Portugal, by an Italian general carrying a false passport. They are conducted in Sicily, by an emissary who comes by aircraft and goes back the same way. They are conducted, in the last days, in a tent in a Sicilian olive grove. On the third of September, nineteen forty-three, an armistice is signed. Italy is to surrender to the Allies. The surrender, however, is to be kept secret for several days, until the Allies can land in force on the Italian mainland and protect the new government from the Germans. This is a fragile arrangement. It does not entirely hold. When the surrender is finally announced, on the radio, on the evening of the eighth of September, the Italian army receives no orders to fight the Germans. Many Italian units simply lay down their arms and go home. Others are disarmed by the Germans before they can react. In Greece, in Yugoslavia, in southern France, where Italian divisions are stationed, the disarming is sometimes peaceful and sometimes not. On the small Greek island of Cephalonia, an Italian division refuses to surrender to the Germans and fights for a week before being overwhelmed; the survivors, more than four thousand men, are shot in groups in the days that follow. The Italian fleet, on the orders of the new government, sails from its bases for Malta to surrender to the Allies; the German air force attacks it on the way and sinks the battleship Roma, with most of her crew, off the coast of Sardinia. The Italian government itself, in Rome, flees the city in cars in the early morning hours of the ninth of September, and reaches the Allied lines at Brindisi, on the heel of the boot, two days later. The King and Badoglio escape with their lives. The country, behind them, is occupied by the Germans within seventy-two hours.

On the same day the armistice is signed, the third of September, the British Eighth Army crosses the Strait of Messina and lands on the toe of Italy. The operation is called Baytown. The crossing is unopposed. The Germans, who have been expecting a landing further north, have already withdrawn from the toe. Montgomery's army moves up the boot of Italy, slowly, on poor coastal roads, with bridges blown by the retreating Germans and supply columns stretching back into Sicily. They will not, in the days that follow, arrive in time to influence what happens at Salerno. A few days later, on the ninth of September, a small British force makes a second supplementary landing at the port of Taranto, on the heel of the boot — Operation Slapstick — and finds the port nearly undefended. The British First Airborne Division comes ashore there, in cruisers, without parachutes, and walks into the city.

The main Allied landing comes on the same day, the ninth of September, nineteen forty-three, at Salerno, on the western coast of Italy, about thirty miles south of Naples. The operation is called Avalanche. The American Fifth Army, commanded by General Mark Clark, goes ashore at dawn, at three points along a thirty-five-mile stretch of beach. The night before, on the radio, the world has heard that Italy has surrendered. The Allied troops in their landing craft have heard it too. There is a feeling, in the boats, that the landing will be unopposed, that the Italians will welcome them, that the Germans will have withdrawn to the north. The feeling is wrong. The Germans, who have been expecting a landing at Salerno for some time, are waiting on the high ground above the beach. The Sixteenth Panzer Division, with about a hundred tanks, holds the heights overlooking the beaches. The first wave that lands is met with artillery and machine-gun fire. The men of the American Sixth Corps and the British Tenth Corps go into the sand under a heavy fire and stay there for most of the day.

On the southern beaches, where the American Thirty-Sixth Division comes ashore at the ancient Greek temples of Paestum, the German fire is heavy but the line is held. On the northern beaches, where the British Tenth Corps lands, the fight is for a string of small fishing villages — Maiori, Vietri, Salerno itself — that the Germans have fortified with machine-gun nests in the houses and artillery in the hills behind. The British Forty-Sixth and Fifty-Sixth Divisions push inland through the streets, building by building. American Rangers and British Commandos, on the far northern flank, take a small mountain pass at Maiori and hold it for nine days against repeated counter-attacks, in some cases at bayonet point. Between the British in the north and the Americans in the south is a stretch of open river plain, the Sele plain, where the Sele and Calore rivers meet. The Germans, identifying the gap, drive an armored thrust into it on the thirteenth of September. They come within a mile and a half of the beach. American artillery, firing over open sights from the sand, stops them. The Thirty-Sixth Division clerks, cooks, and headquarters personnel are pulled into a defensive line that day, with rifles, and stand on the beach in case the line breaks. It does not break. By dusk, the German thrust is halted, and the Sele line is held.

For the first week at Salerno, the beachhead is in real danger. The Germans, under Field Marshal Albert Kesselring, the commander of all German forces in Italy, counter-attack from the high ground every day. They drive the American Thirty-Sixth Division back almost to the water's edge on the thirteenth of September. There is a moment, in those days, when General Clark considers re-embarking part of his army and moving it north or south to a new beach. The order is not given. Reinforcements arrive. The American Eighty-Second Airborne Division drops into the beachhead at night, by parachute, on the night of the thirteenth and fourteenth, jumping into a perimeter no larger than the city of Cleveland. Naval gunfire from the battleships and cruisers offshore, including the British battleships Warspite and Valiant, comes down on the German positions. The Warspite, an old battleship that had fought at Jutland in nineteen sixteen, is hit on the sixteenth of September by a German radio-guided bomb and crawls back to Malta on emergency power. By the sixteenth, the line at Salerno holds. By the eighteenth, the Germans begin to withdraw to the north. The beachhead is secure.

We pause here for a moment. The story will keep going, but if you are still with us, this is a good place to mention that we put a lot of effort into bringing you these stories. If you are enjoying listening, a quiet like helps the channel, and subscribing tells us to make more like this. Thank you for staying with us. The story continues.

On the first of October, nineteen forty-three, the city of Naples is liberated. It is the first major European city to be taken by the Allies in the Second World War. Naples, before the Germans left it, has been thoroughly wrecked. The harbor has been blown up. The water mains have been broken. The sewer system has been broken. Time bombs have been left in the post office and in the army barracks, set to go off days later, after the Allies have moved in. One of those bombs, in the central post office, kills more than seventy soldiers and civilians on the eighth of October. The British and American engineers go to work. Within ten days, the harbor is partially open again, and supply ships are being unloaded. Within a month, it is the busiest port in the Mediterranean. Naples will be the supply base for the Italian campaign for the next eighteen months. From Naples, the front in the mountains to the north can be supplied with food, fuel, ammunition, and replacements. Without Naples, there would be no campaign in Italy.

North of Naples, the country changes. The coastal plain narrows. The Apennine mountains rise, on both sides of the road, in steep wooded ridges. The Volturno River, which runs from east to west across the boot, is the first major obstacle. The Germans hold the north bank. On the night of the twelfth and thirteenth of October, nineteen forty-three, the Fifth Army crosses the Volturno in three places. The crossings are made under fire, in the rain, with engineers building footbridges and pontoon bridges in the dark. The crossings succeed. The Germans, who have been ordered only to delay, withdraw to the next river, and then to the next. The autumn rains begin. The mountain roads turn to mud. The pace of the advance, which had been a few miles a day, slows to a few hundred yards a day.

Through November and December of nineteen forty-three, the Fifth Army inches forward against a series of intermediate German positions known together as the Bernhardt Line. The line uses small mountains, with names that mean nothing to the men crossing them but that they will remember for the rest of their lives — Monte Camino, Monte la Difensa, Monte Sammucro, Monte Lungo. Each mountain is taken by climbing it under fire, in fog and freezing rain, on slopes too steep for vehicles. The American First Special Service Force, a joint American and Canadian commando unit trained for winter mountain warfare, takes Monte la Difensa on the night of the second and third of December, climbing two thousand feet of cliff in the dark and surprising the German garrison at the summit at dawn. The Thirty-Sixth Division, which had landed at Salerno, fights for the village of San Pietro Infine through the second week of December. The village, by the time it is taken, has ceased to exist; the houses are reduced to walls and rubble; the inhabitants who had not fled are sheltering in caves on the hillsides. By the middle of January, nineteen forty-four, after three months of fighting in the mountains, the Allies have moved seventy miles north of Salerno. They have come up against the main German defensive position, which is called the Gustav Line.

The Gustav Line runs across the boot of Italy, from the Tyrrhenian Sea on the west, through the mountains in the middle, to the Adriatic on the east. The line uses three rivers — the Garigliano, the Rapido, and the Sangro — and the high ridges between them. The center of the line, in the high mountains, is anchored on a peak called Monte Cassino, which rises some five hundred meters above the valley. On the top of Monte Cassino is a Benedictine abbey, built in the year five hundred and twenty-nine, fifteen centuries old, one of the oldest monasteries in Christian Europe. The abbey is a very large stone building, visible for miles. The Germans, when they prepared the Gustav Line, made an arrangement with the Vatican that the abbey itself would not be occupied; the German line is built on the slopes below the abbey, using the natural rock and the village of Cassino at the base of the mountain as fortified positions. The arrangement is, in the end, not enough. The Allies, when they reach the line in the middle of January nineteen forty-four, do not move past it for nearly six months.

The first battle of Cassino begins on the seventeenth of January, nineteen forty-four. The British Tenth Corps, on the coast, attacks across the Garigliano River with two divisions and gains a small foothold on the far side. Three days later, on the night of the twentieth and twenty-first of January, the American Thirty-Sixth Division attempts to cross the Rapido River, in front of the town of Cassino, in the dark. The crossing is a disaster. The river is in flood, swollen with winter rain, running fast and cold. The boats are swept away. Smoke pots that the engineers have set up to screen the crossings are blown back into the men's faces. The Germans, on the high ground, fire down into the water, where smoke and flares light the river. By dawn, two regiments of the Thirty-Sixth have been destroyed. The division loses more than two thousand men in two days. The crossing is called off. The line, on the Rapido, is not broken. After the war, the Texas Thirty-Sixth, which lost so many of its sons that night, will petition the United States Congress for an investigation into who gave the order. There will be hearings. There will be no conclusion that anyone is to blame. The men of the Thirty-Sixth, the survivors, will go on to fight in the second and third battles of Cassino, and the fourth, and at Anzio, and in the Vosges in France, and into Germany. Many of them will not.

Four days after the Rapido disaster, on the twenty-second of January, nineteen forty-four, the Allies attempt to outflank the Gustav Line by sea. The American Sixth Corps, commanded by Major General John Lucas, lands at a small resort town on the coast called Anzio, sixty miles north of Cassino and only thirty-five miles south of Rome. The operation is called Shingle. The landing, like the first hours at Salerno, is a great surprise to the Germans. The beach is almost undefended. There are no German divisions within fifty miles of Anzio when the first troops come ashore. The road to Rome, in the first hours, is open. By midday, the Sixth Corps has thirty-six thousand men ashore and has lost only thirteen killed.

General Lucas, who has been told to consolidate his beachhead before pushing inland, consolidates. He digs in. He builds up his stocks. He waits. The decision is one of the most argued-about decisions of the entire war. Lucas himself wrote later that he believed the beachhead was too small and his force too weak to make a thrust toward Rome that could be sustained against the inevitable German counter-attack; that to try would have been to risk the destruction of the corps. His critics, including Churchill, have argued that the road was open and should have been taken. By the time he is ready to advance, ten days later, Field Marshal Kesselring has performed one of the great improvisations of the war: he has moved seven divisions to the area around Anzio, by rail and road, from northern Italy and from southern France, and the road to Rome is closed. The Anzio beachhead, which was supposed to break the Gustav Line by going around it, becomes another beachhead under siege.

For the next four months, the men at Anzio will live in foxholes in a flat, marshy plain that the Germans, in the surrounding hills called the Alban Hills, can see into from every direction. There is no rear area at Anzio. Every part of the beachhead is in artillery range. Every supply ship that comes in is in artillery range. Every field hospital is in artillery range. The Germans send their largest railway gun, a long-barreled cannon the soldiers call Anzio Annie, to fire on the harbor. The shells from Anzio Annie are so heavy that men in the beachhead can hear them coming for the entire forty-five seconds of their flight. The men dig their holes deeper. They line them with wood from blown-up buildings. They cover them with sandbags and railway ties. They stay in them for weeks at a time.

In February of nineteen forty-four, the Germans attempt to drive the beachhead into the sea. The operation is called Fischfang. It is delivered against the British First Division and the American Forty-Fifth Division on the central part of the beachhead, around a small village called Aprilia, which the soldiers call the Factory because of a large industrial-style building at its center. For three days and three nights, the Germans push into the British and American lines. The lines bend, in places, almost back to the beach. The defenders fight from buildings, from caves, from a dry stream bed called the Wadi. The British First Division, on the night of the seventeenth and eighteenth of February, holds a line on a small set of caves, with what is left of two infantry battalions, against three German regiments, and does not give way. The line holds. By the twentieth of February, Fischfang is over. The Germans have not broken the beachhead. But neither have the men in the beachhead broken out.

In early February, while Fischfang is being fought, the Allies make a second attempt at Cassino. The town, which lies in the valley below the abbey, is to be taken by frontal assault. The fighting is house to house. The Germans, who have brought paratroopers — some of the best infantry in the German army — to defend the town, hold every street. The American Thirty-Fourth Division, in the mountains above the town, climbs to within four hundred yards of the abbey wall and is stopped there for two weeks by snow, fog, and German fire. After two weeks, the assault is called off. The line has not moved. On the fifteenth of February, nineteen forty-four, the Allies bomb the abbey on the top of Monte Cassino. Two hundred and fifty heavy bombers drop nearly six hundred tons of explosives on the building. The abbey, which had been declared a neutral zone and which the Germans had not, in fact, been using, is reduced to rubble. After the bombing, the Germans, who had been respecting the abbey from outside, move into the rubble, which is now an excellent defensive position, full of cover and fields of fire. The third battle of Cassino, in March, attempts to take the rubble. The New Zealand Corps, with troops from New Zealand, India, and Britain, attacks the town and the rubble for ten days, in cooperation with what is, at that time, the heaviest aerial bombing of any single tactical target in the war up to that date. The line still does not move. By the end of March, after three battles for Cassino, the front has gained nothing. The dead lie in the rubble of the town, and on the slopes of the mountain, and in the fields beside the Rapido, where the snow comes and goes through March and April.

We pause here again. We put a lot of effort into bringing you these stories. If listening has helped you to rest, a quiet like helps us reach more people, and subscribing tells us to make more like this. Sleep well, if you are sleeping. The story continues.

Over the spring of nineteen forty-four, the Allied commanders in Italy, working under General Sir Harold Alexander, plan a fourth attack on the Gustav Line. The plan is called Diadem. The idea is to attack the line in great strength, all along its length, simultaneously, with both the Fifth Army and the Eighth Army, and to break it not by frontal assault on the rubble of Cassino but by a wide turning movement through the mountains to the south, around the German left flank. The Eighth Army, which had been on the Adriatic coast for the winter, is moved across the spine of Italy, in great secrecy, to the Cassino front, doubling the strength of the assault. The breakthrough force, in the mountains south of Cassino, is to be the French Expeditionary Corps, commanded by General Alphonse Juin. The French force includes Moroccan and Algerian troops, a corps of mountain soldiers called the Goumiers, who are accustomed to high ground and who carry their supplies on mules. The Goumiers, who have not been used in significant numbers before in the campaign, are about to do something that the planners on both sides have considered impossible.

Operation Diadem begins on the night of the eleventh and twelfth of May, nineteen forty-four. Two thousand Allied guns fire along a twenty-five-mile front for forty minutes. The infantry advances at midnight. In the lower country, in front of Cassino, the British Thirteenth Corps and the Polish Second Corps attack the rubble of the abbey. The Polish Second Corps, commanded by General Vladislav Anders, is composed of soldiers who have come a very long way to be here. Many of them were taken prisoner by the Soviets in nineteen thirty-nine, after the partition of Poland; released in nineteen forty-one, after the German invasion of Russia; marched out of Russia, through Persia, to the Mediterranean; trained in Egypt; and brought to Italy. They have come, by their reckoning, eight thousand miles to fight for the freedom of a country, Poland, that they will not see again. Their first attack, on the twelfth of May, is broken on the slopes below the abbey, with very heavy losses. They reorganize. They attack again, on the seventeenth. They take the rubble of Monte Cassino on the eighteenth of May, nineteen forty-four. The Polish flag is raised on the abbey at sunrise, alongside the British. A bugler plays the old trumpet call of Krakow over the ruins. The fourth battle of Cassino is over.

In the mountains to the south, on the same nights, the French Expeditionary Corps and the Goumiers do what was not expected. They move through the Aurunci Mountains, which the Germans had considered impassable, on goat tracks and dry stream beds, often with no roads at all. They move at night. They carry their food, ammunition, and water on mule trains that follow the infantry by hours. By the eighteenth of May, when the Polish flag is raised on Cassino, the Goumiers are already eight miles into the German rear. The Gustav Line has been turned. The next German line, the Hitler Line, called by the Germans the Senger Line, is broken on the twenty-third of May. The Tenth German Army, which has held the line at Cassino for six months, is in a general retreat to the north.

At Anzio, on the twenty-third of May, the Sixth Corps, now commanded by Major General Lucian Truscott — who had replaced Lucas in February — breaks out of the beachhead. The plan, which has been agreed with General Alexander in advance, is for the Sixth Corps to drive eastward and cut the only good road that leads from Cassino to Rome — Highway Six, the Via Casilina, which runs through a small town called Valmontone. If the cut is made, the entire Tenth German Army, retreating up that road, can be destroyed. The breakout begins well. The Third Infantry Division, on the first day, takes more casualties than any American division has taken in a single day in the war up to that date — nine hundred and fifty killed, wounded, and missing. They take the small town of Cisterna by the twenty-fifth of May. By the thirtieth, the Sixth Corps is approaching Highway Six. And then General Mark Clark, in command of the Fifth Army, changes the order. He turns the Sixth Corps northwest, away from Highway Six, and toward Rome. The reasons for the order have been argued about by historians for eighty years. Clark, in his memoirs, says that he believed the German road was already covered by other forces; others have written that he wanted his American army to take Rome before the British could do so. The argument is not for tonight. What matters is that the road is not cut. The Tenth German Army, retreating up Highway Six, escapes to the north and lives to fight on the next line.

On the fourth of June, nineteen forty-four, American troops of the Fifth Army enter Rome. They are the first soldiers of any Western army to enter the city since it was last fought over more than a thousand years before. The crowds line the streets. There are flowers on the tanks. The German garrison has withdrawn the night before, declaring Rome an open city. There is no fighting in the streets. The Italian campaign, after eight long months of attrition, has produced a famous victory. It is on the front pages of the American papers for two days.

On the sixth of June, two days later, the Allies land in Normandy. Italy disappears from the front pages and from public attention. From this date, for the rest of the war, the Italian campaign will be the secondary front, the holding action, the place where divisions are not sent. Seven of the best Allied divisions in Italy are pulled out, in the summer of nineteen forty-four, for an invasion of southern France called Operation Dragoon. The American Sixth Corps, which had broken out of Anzio, leaves Italy. The French Expeditionary Corps, which had broken the Gustav Line in the Aurunci Mountains, leaves Italy. The campaign in Italy goes on, with what is left, against a German army that has just withdrawn to a new and stronger line in the Apennines, two hundred miles to the north.

Through June and July of nineteen forty-four, the Allies pursue the retreating Germans up the Italian peninsula. They cross the Trasimene Line, in the rolling country of Umbria, where Hannibal once defeated a Roman army by ambush, two thousand and twenty years before. They cross the Arno River. They liberate the city of Florence on the fourth of August. The Germans, before leaving Florence, blow up every bridge over the Arno except one — the Ponte Vecchio, the medieval covered bridge — which they spare, perhaps on the personal order of Hitler, who had visited Florence as a young man before the First World War and admired it. The buildings on either end of the Ponte Vecchio, however, are destroyed, and the streets approaching the bridge are made impassable, so that the bridge itself, though intact, is an island for a time. The retreat is well-conducted by the Germans. Every other bridge is blown. Every road is mined. Every farmhouse on the high ground holds a machine gun until the last possible moment. The pursuit averages, in good weather, perhaps three or four miles a day. In the mountains, less than that.

In front of the Allies now is the Gothic Line, the Linea Gotica, the last great German defensive line in Italy. The Gothic Line runs from the Tyrrhenian coast near Pisa, through the highest part of the central Apennines, to the Adriatic coast near Pesaro. The line has been built, over the spring and summer, by Italian and German labor battalions, with barbed wire, anti-tank ditches, minefields, and steel turrets dug into the hilltops. The Germans had named it, originally, the Gothic Line; in the late summer, on Hitler's order, it was renamed the Green Line, to make a possible withdrawal less dramatic in the event the line was breached. The men in the field, on both sides, continued to call it Gothic. The mountains here are higher than at Cassino. The passes are narrower. The weather, in the autumn that is coming, will be worse.

The Allied attack on the Gothic Line begins in late August of nineteen forty-four. The British Eighth Army, on the Adriatic coast, attacks first, with eight divisions, near the small republic of San Marino. The plan is to attract German reserves to the Adriatic, then attack with the Fifth Army in the central mountains where the Germans are now thinner. The Eighth Army, in two weeks, fights through the line and reaches the city of Rimini. The fighting in front of Rimini, on a feature called Coriano Ridge, is the heaviest the Eighth Army has fought since El Alamein. They take Rimini on the twenty-first of September. The country in front of them, the Romagna, is supposed to be flat tank country leading to the Po Valley. It is not. It is cut by canals and dikes and small rivers, every few miles, and behind every river is a German rearguard, and the autumn rains have begun. The Eighth Army's pursuit, planned for September, becomes another series of crossings of small rivers in mud, in October and November. The Senio. The Lamone. The Ronco. The Savio. By the end of December, the Eighth Army has not reached the Po.

The American Fifth Army, in the central mountains, attacks two weeks after the Eighth, through two passes called the Futa and the Il Giogo. By the end of September, the Fifth Army has penetrated the line, in places, to a depth of fifteen or twenty miles. They are within ten miles of Bologna, the great city on the southern edge of the Po Valley. They do not reach it. The Germans, however, have not been broken. They have fallen back to a second line, in the mountains, just south of Bologna. And in the first week of October, the autumn rains begin in earnest. They do not stop, with any consistency, for the next six months.

The winter of nineteen forty-four to forty-five, in the Italian Apennines, is the third winter of the campaign. It is the worst. The mountains are five and six thousand feet high. The snow lies deep on the upper slopes from November until April. The roads, where there are roads, are narrow tracks that can be cut by a single landslide. Supplies, in the high country, move on the backs of mules. The Tenth Mountain Division of the United States Army, which arrives at the front in January of nineteen forty-five, finds itself supplied by mule trains that climb three thousand feet from the valley each night, in the dark, in the snow, with no lights. The Tenth Mountain is a unit specifically trained for mountain warfare, with skis, with ice axes, with technical climbing rope; it is the only such unit in the American army; it has been kept in reserve in Colorado for two years waiting for a use. It is given, in the Apennines, the very high ridge called Riva Ridge, and the mountain called Monte Belvedere, both of which the Germans have been holding through the winter and which have repulsed three previous Allied attacks. On the night of the eighteenth and nineteenth of February, nineteen forty-five, the Tenth Mountain climbs the back side of Riva Ridge in the dark, in silence, on technical mountain rope, on a face the Germans have considered unclimbable. They take the ridge from the Germans before dawn. Three days later, they take Monte Belvedere. The mountain warriors of the Tenth, in those weeks, do what no other Allied unit in Italy has been able to do, which is to fight on the highest ground and to win.

Elsewhere on the line, through that winter, the front is largely static. The British Eighth Army, on the Adriatic plain, has crossed several rivers to reach the outskirts of Ravenna, which is liberated on the fourth of December. The Brazilian Expeditionary Force, the only Latin American ground unit in the European war, takes a series of mountain villages near the town of Pistoia and, in February, takes the high ground at Monte Castello, a feature the Allies have been trying to take for four months. The Brazilians, twenty-five thousand strong, fight through the winter alongside the Tenth Mountain and the American Ninety-Second Division, which is composed of African American soldiers under, in many cases, white officers, and which fights in the western mountains, near the marble quarries of Carrara. The Ninety-Second clears the coastal mountains down to the sea by the early spring. On the Adriatic flank, in March, the British Royal Marines and units of the Special Air Service conduct an unusual amphibious operation across the lagoon at Lake Comacchio, in flat-bottomed assault boats, to seize the spit of land between the lake and the sea. It is one of the last commando operations of the European war.

In the German-held part of Italy, in the winter of nineteen forty-four to forty-five, an Italian civil war is taking place. After Mussolini was rescued from his arrest by German paratroopers in September of nineteen forty-three — the Germans had located him in his mountain hotel and landed gliders on the meadow outside, taking him out by light aircraft to Vienna — the Germans installed him as the head of a new fascist state in the north of Italy, called the Italian Social Republic, with its capital at the small town of Salò on Lake Garda. The republic has the form of a government but no real power; the Germans run the country, and the Italian Social Republic forces, the Decima MAS and the Black Brigades, fight as auxiliaries on the German side. Against the republic, in the mountains, the Italian Resistance — the partisan movement known as the CLN — has been growing. By the winter of nineteen forty-four, there are perhaps a hundred thousand armed partisans operating in the mountains and in the cities of northern Italy. They cut railway lines. They ambush German supply columns. They hold, in places, entire valleys, called partisan republics, of which the most famous is the small Republic of the Ossola, near the Swiss border, which existed for forty days in the autumn of nineteen forty-four before being reoccupied. The Germans, with the help of the fascist Italian Social Republic, conduct reprisals. The reprisals are severe. Whole villages are burned. Civilians are shot in groups of ten or a hundred. The names of these places — Marzabotto, where seven hundred and seventy people were killed in the autumn of nineteen forty-four; Sant'Anna di Stazzema, where five hundred and sixty were killed in August of that year; the Ardeatine Caves outside Rome, where three hundred and thirty-five Italian civilians were shot in March of nineteen forty-four in reprisal for a partisan attack on a German police battalion — will be remembered in Italy long after the war ends. They are not the subject of tonight's story, but they are part of what is happening in the country, on the other side of the line, while the Allies wait for the spring.

The spring offensive in Italy begins on the ninth of April, nineteen forty-five. It is called Operation Grapeshot. By this date, the war in the rest of Europe is nearly over. The Russians are on the Oder, twenty miles from Berlin. The Western Allies have crossed the Rhine and are deep into central Germany. The end is in sight, in a way that it has not been in sight before. In Italy, the Allies have nearly thirty divisions on the line; the Germans have twenty-three, but most of them are below strength, short of fuel, short of ammunition, and aware that the war is lost. The Allied air forces have been bombing German supply lines and bridges across the Po River for months, in an operation called Strangle, and the German army in Italy is, by April, an army that cannot move during the day. The attack, on the ninth of April, opens with twenty minutes of artillery fire and four hours of bombing along the Eighth Army front, on the Adriatic plain. By the next day, the Eighth Army is across the Senio River, the line on which they had been stuck for months. By the fifteenth of April, the Eighth Army is across the Santerno. The Fifth Army, in the mountains, attacks on the fourteenth and is into the mountains north of Bologna by the seventeenth. The Tenth Mountain Division, which had taken Riva Ridge in February, leads the breakthrough into the Po Valley.

The city of Bologna, the great prize of the central Italian front, is liberated on the twenty-first of April. The Polish Second Corps, the same corps that took Monte Cassino a year before, enters the city from the south at sunrise. By that afternoon, American troops have entered from the southwest. The Germans, for the first time in the campaign, are not falling back to a new line but coming apart altogether. North of Bologna is the Po Valley, the great flat agricultural plain of northern Italy, which extends for a hundred miles to the foot of the Alps. The Po River, the largest river in Italy, runs from west to east across the valley. Behind the Po, the Germans had hoped to hold a final line. They do not reach it.

The race across the Po Valley, from the twenty-first of April through the twenty-eighth, is the fastest movement of the entire campaign. American armored columns of the Fifth Army cross the Po on the twenty-third of April, having found the bridges destroyed and crossing in DUKW amphibious trucks and rubber boats. They take Verona on the twenty-fifth. They reach the southern shore of Lake Garda on the twenty-sixth. The British Eighth Army crosses the Po further east and takes Padua on the twenty-eighth. By this point, the German army in Italy is no longer an army. Its units have surrendered, or melted into the countryside, or are being rounded up by Italian partisans in the towns. In Milan, in Turin, in Genoa, in the days from the twenty-fifth to the twenty-eighth of April, the partisans rise and take the cities themselves, before the Allies arrive. Milan is liberated on the twenty-fifth of April by the partisans of the CLN, and the day is remembered, in Italy, as Liberation Day, the Festa della Liberazione, every year since.

On the twenty-eighth of April, partisans capture Mussolini, who is attempting to flee with a German convoy toward Switzerland, dressed in a German army overcoat. He is taken to a small village on the shore of Lake Como and shot the next morning, alongside his mistress and several of his ministers. The bodies are taken to Milan and hung, by the heels, from the steel framework of a half-built petrol station in a square called the Piazzale Loreto, where Italian civilians had been executed by the Fascists the year before. The crowd in the square is large. Photographs of the hanging are printed, in the days that follow, in newspapers around the world. The war in Italy, by the end of the month, is effectively over.

The formal surrender of the German forces in Italy is signed on the twenty-ninth of April, nineteen forty-five, at the headquarters of Field Marshal Sir Harold Alexander in the Royal Palace of Caserta, north of Naples — the same palace that General Clark had used as his headquarters eighteen months before. The surrender takes effect on the second of May, nineteen forty-five. Just under a million German soldiers in Italy lay down their arms. It is the first general surrender of a German army in the Second World War, predating the surrender of all of Germany by six days. On the eighth of May, all of Germany surrenders. The war in Europe is over.

The Italian campaign, in the final accounting, lasted six hundred and four days. It cost the Allies more than three hundred thousand casualties — killed, wounded, captured, and missing. It cost the Germans, by their own count, more than four hundred thousand. It cost the Italian civilian population, in deaths from bombing, from reprisal, from starvation, and from collateral fire, perhaps a hundred and fifty thousand more. It tied down twenty-three German divisions, through the year of the Normandy invasion and the year of the Rhine crossings, that might have fought elsewhere. Whether the campaign was worth what it cost has been debated, since nineteen forty-five, by historians and by the men who fought in it. The men who fought in it, when asked, often answered that it was a long campaign in hard country, that the Germans were good soldiers, that the mountains were terrible, that the rain was worse, and that they had been forgotten, by the people back home, after the sixth of June, nineteen forty-four. The forgetting, in part, is what tonight's story is about. The men in the Italian mountains — the Polish and the French Moroccans and the Indians and the New Zealanders and the South Africans and the Brazilians and the Americans of the Tenth Mountain and the British of the Eighth Army and the Canadians of the First Canadian Corps and the Italians who fought, by the end of the campaign, alongside the Allies in their own reorganized army of the south — they do not enter the story of the Second World War in the way that the men of Normandy enter it. They are at a different front, in a different geography, against a different mission. The mission was to hold the German divisions in place, and the mission was carried out, in mud and snow and rock, for twenty months.

The abbey of Monte Cassino, which was bombed flat in February of nineteen forty-four, was rebuilt after the war by the Italian state, on the same plan, with money from the Italian government and from international donors, in the years from nineteen forty-eight to nineteen sixty-four. The abbey today looks, from the road, almost exactly as it did before the war. The cemeteries on the slopes below it — the Polish cemetery, with its eight hundred graves and its inscription saying that for our freedom and yours the soldiers of Poland gave their souls to God, their bodies to Italy, and their hearts to Poland; the Commonwealth cemetery, with the four thousand graves of the British and the New Zealanders and the Indians; the German cemetery, with the twenty thousand graves of the men who held the line; the French and Moroccan cemetery, just to the south — are quiet places. Visitors come, in the spring, when the wildflowers are out on the mountain. The Anzio beachhead, where the Sixth Corps lived in foxholes for four months, is today a beach with hotels and pasta restaurants and the Tyrrhenian Sea coming in slowly on the sand; there is a small museum near the harbor. The Po Valley, which was crossed in seven days at the end of April nineteen forty-five, is once again the agricultural heart of Italy, with its long rows of poplar trees and its flat, mist-covered fields and the slow wide brown river running east toward the Adriatic. The mountains of the Apennines, the long stone spine of Italy, are still there. They will always be there. They will, in the centuries that come, be fought over again, perhaps, by other armies, in other wars; or, perhaps, never again. The story of one war, in those mountains, is the story we have told tonight.

The rivers are quiet. The Volturno is quiet. The Garigliano is quiet. The Rapido is quiet, where the Thirty-Sixth Division was destroyed in a single night. The Senio and the Santerno, which the Eighth Army crossed in the spring offensive, run quietly to the Adriatic. The Po, the great river of the north, runs slowly to the sea, between its low green dykes. The roads in the mountains are open again, and the bridges have all been rebuilt. The men who were lost on both sides are at peace, in the cemeteries on the hillsides, in the small towns whose names appear on the headstones — towns in Poland, in England, in Texas, in Bavaria, in Algeria, in Brazil, in New Zealand, in India, in Canada, in South Africa, in Italy itself. The men who came home from Italy are mostly gone now too, of old age, in the long years that have followed. The mountains they crossed are still there. The names of the rivers they crossed have not changed. The wildflowers, in the spring, come up through the grass on the slopes below the rebuilt abbey, and on the cliffs above Anzio, and along the dykes of the Po, year after year, as if the war had never been there at all.
